Thank you for submitting the paper "Population-level asymmetry of the cerebral cortex: reproducibility, lifespan changes, heritability, and individual differences" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and a Senior Editor. The following individual involved in the review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Dorothy V M Bishop (Reviewer #3).

Comments to the Authors:

We are sorry to say that, after consultation with the reviewers, we have decided that this work in its current form will not be considered further for publication by eLife.

However, note that in the light of the very constructive comment and in tune with our general belief that these data can potentially provide an important reference for future studies, we as editors would be willing to consider a future, thoroughly revised revision of this paper. We would treat it as a new submission (with potentially new reviewers being invited, depending on the availability of reviewers.) – All of this of course depending on the nature and extent of your revisions to the manuscript and your documentation of these. *

Specifically, the reviewers and editors agreed that the paper provides a useful descriptive catalogue of phenomena related to hemispheric anatomical asymmetries and that it does so in a largely sound manner (but see specific methodological concerns below). However, there was no consensus to be reached that this study has a specific impact on our learning about the mechanisms of hemispheric lateralisation. After reviews and an elaborate discussion amongst reviewers and editors, concerns remained over the mechanistic impact of the results presented and the degree of conceptual synthesis provided, so we decided not to invite a revision of this study for eLife.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

I have several comments and suggestions that I hope will be of use to the authors.

1. In discussing the differences between regional asymmetries in cortical thickness and cortical area, it is prudent to mention that CT is less reliable than SA and this reliability difference may be amplified in the computation of asymmetry.

2. In claiming that "disrupted cortical asymmetry is a confirmed feature of… aging…" the authors cite one study and ignore others that not only lend little support to this conclusion but also warn that regional asymmetry in the aging brain is not well-replicated even across similar samples.

3. Unclear how GAMM captures nonlinearity of change over time with only two measurement occasions.

4. Discovering a capture of 21% of common variance by the first component of the PCA hardly signals the existence of a single factor. CFA would be a more appropriate way of testing single vs multiple factors hypotheses.

5. The authors consistently characterize correlations as "strong" – unclear why. The characterization is somewhat hyperbolic: for example, r=.56 does not seem particularly strong, with about 70% of the variance not shared by the variables. Why not just write "correlated," report the magnitude and the direction and let the readers make a qualitative judgment if they feel like it.

Some stylistic editing will improve this manuscript. For example, the sentence "Areal asymmetry correlates in specific regions…" in the Abstract is quite unwieldy and can be split into two or three.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

I found some of the graphs hard to read.

For example, in Figure 5 the color scale was hard to read. It goes from one shade of blue to another shade of blue and I could not really see much distinction.

Figure 6, it is not clear what is being plotted on the abscissa. There is no axis label.

The authors use the term "longitudinal" to describe their age-related analyses, but my understanding of that term is that it refers to the same individuals tested over time, which is not the case here; it's a cross-sectional approach.

The word "course" should be "coarse" (line 70).

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

Overall, while I think the attempt at a comprehensive approach by the authors is commendable, the paper, which includes a great deal of supplementary material, is just too dense and unwieldy. My recommendation would be to break it up. I'm not a fan of authors who turn papers into 'minimal publishable units', but here we have the opposite – a paper so dense with information that it is hard to follow.

I don't know if eLife would consider a series of related papers like this but the work would be easier to follow, and potentially more influential if it were split up. There is a nice logical progression, with the initial analyses delineating brain areas that are consistently asymmetric, and subsequent analyses then using these, so a series of papers would work well I think – something like this:

Paper 1: qs 1 and 3 – replicability of population-level asymmetries, and inter-regional correlations.

Paper 2: consideration of causal factors, incorporating longitudinal analysis of lifespan trajectories of asymmetry (q2) and heritability (q4). The longitudinal analysis could potentially incorporate analysis of interregional correlations across age – given that connectivity changes with age, there is a rationale for looking at that (LCBC sample), but even without that, this would make a meaty paper.

Paper 3 (q5) Consideration of significance of individual differences in terms of correlations with sex, handedness, and general cognitive ability (UKB sample). Potentially more could be done with this; it could look at associations with absolute as well as raw asymmetry indices. But I think it would be most valuable if preceded by a balanced review of prior work in this area, culminating in a list of claims of associations that could be tested in this sample. That would make it more evident which claims are NOT supported, which would be very useful for the field.

Note: I am not recommending jettisoning the null results – on the contrary, I would like to see them given more serious treatment, as they could be helpful in moving the field forward.

Since breaking up the paper this way would be a fairly radical move, I'll assume that the authors and/or editors will decide against this, and so my remaining comments will be written as if we are dealing with a paper that does incorporate all the current material.

I would suggest rewriting the Abstract to give a more balanced account of the findings, including an indication of the null as well as positive results.

I don't know whether eLife insists on the particular structuring of the paper used here, with Methods at the end. I would hope this could be modified, as for a multi-question paper like this, it is particularly frustrating for the reader. The introduction ends with five specific questions clearly laid out, but we then jump into Results, which are hard to understand without seeing the Methods. So the reader goes forward to Methods, where the dataset for each of the five questions is first described, then the data analysis methods for each of the five questions. This involves a great deal of jumping about. I found myself wanting to literally cut and paste the material so I could read it in a sensible sequence.

Interregional correlations

The material on interregional correlations was fascinating but hard to follow. The numbers (Figure 4 Figure supplement 1) are hard to read, but I was very surprised at just how low these correlations were for SA, given that people have tended to interpret asymmetries in terms of a general 'torque' effect.

The CT asymmetries were hard to interpret, given the relatively low Mantel scores – and the way the Biobank data stand out even just on the heatmap. This made me wonder if the more restricted age range of the Biobank sample might affect the covariances. I wasn't sure how the age residualisation worked, and whether it was within-sample or across samples, so hard to know if and how the fact that Biobank has a much higher age minimum than others might have an effect?

One thing that makes the results confusing is the flipping of the hemisphere so that the emphasis is on strength of laterality in the population direction. It would be worth taking some time in the introduction to discuss predictions from the 'multifactorial' account versus a 'single factor' account – relating this to discussions of cerebral torque.

An alternative approach would be to just present the unflipped data, explaining that a positive correlation then indicates agreement in left-wardness (regardless of whether the population bias is left or right), and a negative correlation indicates agreement between the strength of lateralisation in the population direction.

The subsequent discussion of these results was pretty clear – it's just the account in Results that was hard to follow.

Heritability

The account of results in the Abstract again focused on the positive findings and ignored the null results as if they were of no interest.

So the Abstract states: "Areal asymmetry is moderately heritable (max h2SNP ~19%), and phenotypic correlations are reflected by high genetic correlations, whereas heritability of thickness asymmetry is low. "

My reading of the results is that none of the twin-based heritability estimates – either global or regional – was statistically significant. Consistent with previous reports by Eyler et al. and others, the strongest influence on asymmetry indices is the E-term (nonshared environment), which may be interpreted in this context as chance (stochastic) influences.

The SNP-based estimates from UK Biobank give a handful of significant heritability estimates for the SA asymmetry, but none for CT. I agree it is of interest to document these, but the genetic effects that are found are not high (19% is the highest estimate, with the remaining 80% of variance accounted for by the e2 term).

I guess it is a case of one's perspective, but my take on this is not "isn't it interesting that if we have a huge sample we can pick up some small genetic effects on a handful of asymmetry measures", but rather, "isn't it interesting that brains end up with similar patterns of structural asymmetry, even though genes explain so little individual variation ". This does suggest that there are genetic influences that create these general biases to one direction or the other, but which have reached fixation in the population and so show little individual variation.

Associations with cognition

As noted above, I felt this treatment was too brief. There is a rich literature on associations with asymmetry for the variables considered here, much of it focusing on the degree rather than the direction of asymmetry. So I would like to see a separate paper dealing with associations with AIs from this analysis, relating the findings more systematically to prior studies.

The discussion did a phenomenal job in pulling everything together but would benefit from some subheadings.

claims.claim: In these clusters, asymmetry development was generally evident until a peak in early adulthood (median age at peak = 24.3) for both leftward and rightward clusters.

claims.claim: 95% of clusters exhibited small but significant asymmetry at age ~4.

claims.claim: Across clusters delineated here we observed little evidence aging-related change from 30 to 89 years corresponded to a relative hemispheric difference in the rate of aging-related thinning, except in regions overlapping with our previous report.

claims.claim: We found a correlation of r=–0.61 between mean asymmetry across all leftward vs. mean asymmetry across all rightward clusters in UKB.

claims.source: For thickness, males exhibited more rightward asymmetry in STS and posterior insula, more leftward thickness asymmetry in superior frontal cortex, but reduced rightward thickness asymmetry in entorhinal cortex and anterior insula, and reduced leftward asymmetry in caudal superior frontal cortex.

claims.claim: Our vertex-wise analysis of cortical asymmetries that reproduce across adult cohorts replicates and completes a recent low-resolution meta-analysis.

claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the results in relation to prior literature.

claims.claim: The marked consistency across samples suggests consensus may now be reached regarding cortical asymmetry phenotypes in humans.
claims.source: The marked consistency across samples suggests consensus may now be reached regarding cortical asymmetry phenotypes in humans, as our results agree with most reported results for areal asymmetry (Kong et al., 2018; Chiarello et al., 2016; Lyttelton et al., 2009; Maingault et al., 2016; Li et al., 2014), as well as several, typically more recent reports for thickness asymmetry (Kong et al., 2018; Roe et al., 2021; Li et al., 2015; Plessen et al., 2014; but see Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Limitations for an outstanding issue regarding the biological origin of thickness asymmetry).
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the results in relation to prior literature.

claims.claim: The high overlap in effects between seven datasets from four countries here suggests these results likely apply universally.
claims.source: The high overlap in effects between seven datasets from four countries here suggests these results likely apply universally.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the replication across multiple international datasets.

claims.claim: This evident consensus suggests genetic-developmental programs regulate mean brain lateralization with respect to both area and apparent thickness in humans.
claims.source: This evident consensus suggests genetic-developmental programs regulate mean brain lateralization with respect to both area and apparent thickness in humans.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the consistency of asymmetry patterns across samples.

claims.claim: The genetic findings presented herein suggest these may have reached population fixation, as heritability of even our optimally delineated asymmetry measures was generally low.
claims.source: However, the genetic findings presented herein suggest these may have reached population fixation, as heritability of even our optimally delineated asymmetry measures was generally low.

claims.claim: This indicates either subject-specific stochastic mechanisms in early neurodevelopment or later developmental influences primarily determine cortical asymmetry.
claims.source: This indicates either subject-specific stochastic mechanisms in early neurodevelopment or later developmental influences primarily determine cortical asymmetry.

claims.claim: One interpretation of lifespan stability combined with low heritability may be stochastic early-life developmental influences determine individual differences in areal asymmetry more than later developmental change.
claims.source: One interpretation of lifespan stability combined with low heritability may be stochastic early-life developmental influences determine individual differences in areal asymmetry more than later developmental change, but work linking prenatal and childhood trajectories is needed to affirm this.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the combined findings.

claims.claim: Childhood development of thickness asymmetry until a peak around age ~24, higher directional variability in adult samples, and lower heritability all converge to suggest thickness asymmetry may be more shaped through subject-specific effects in later childhood, possibly through interaction with the environment.
claims.source: In contrast, childhood development of thickness asymmetry until a peak around age ~24 (Roe et al., 2021), higher directional variability in adult samples, and lower heritability all converge to suggest thickness asymmetry may be more shaped through subject-specific effects in later childhood, possibly through interaction with the environment.
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined findings for thickness asymmetry.

claims.claim: This interpretation applied to asymmetry also agrees with work suggesting cortical area in general may trace more to early-life factors whereas thickness may be more impacted by lifespan influences.
claims.source: This interpretation applied to asymmetry also agrees with work suggesting cortical area in general may trace more to early-life factors (Walhovd et al., 2016; Grasby et al., 2020; Rakic, 1995) whereas thickness may be more impacted by lifespan influences (Grasby et al., 2020; Fjell et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: For areal asymmetry, adult-like patterns of lateralization were strongly established before age ~4, indicating areal asymmetry traces back further and does not primarily emerge through later cortical expansion.
claims.source: For areal asymmetry, adult-like patterns of lateralization were strongly established before age ~4, indicating areal asymmetry traces back further and does not primarily emerge through later cortical expansion (Wierenga et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the lifespan trajectory findings.

claims.claim: This may align with evidence indicating areal asymmetry may be primarily determined in utero.
claims.source: This may align with evidence indicating areal asymmetry may be primarily determined in utero (Li et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2023), including evidence suggesting little change in areal asymmetry from birth to 2 years (Li et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013; Wierenga et al., 2014), and little difference between maps derived from neonates and adults (Li et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: It may also fit with the principle that the primary microstructural basis of cortical area – the number of and spacing between cortical minicolumns – is determined in prenatal life.
claims.source: It may also fit with the principle that the primary microstructural basis of cortical area (Rakic, 1995) – the number of and spacing between cortical minicolumns – is determined in prenatal life (Rakic, 1995; Fjell et al., 2019), and agree with work suggesting asymmetry at this microstructural level may underly hemispheric differences in surface area (Chance et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Our results may therefore constrain the extent to which areal asymmetry can be viewed as a plastic feature of brain organization.

results.result: Population-level cortical asymmetries are highly consistent across seven independent datasets from four countries. Areal asymmetries show high spatial correlation (r=0.88-0.97) with leftward asymmetry in supramarginal gyrus/perisylvian regions and rightward asymmetry in cingulate, inferior parietal cortex, and STS. Thickness asymmetries show an anterior-posterior pattern with more variable spatial correlations (r=0.33-0.93), with consistent leftward asymmetry in cingulate, postcentral gyrus, and superior frontal cortex, and rightward asymmetry in STS, insula, and lingual gyrus.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C35 provide converging evidence from multiple datasets showing replicable patterns of cortical asymmetry. The spatial correlation analyses (C28, C33) and overlapping effects across datasets (C29, C30, C34) demonstrate robust population-level asymmetries. The consistency of individual lateralization proportions across datasets (C35) further supports the reliability of these findings. The results are well-documented with quantitative metrics and visual evidence from Figure 1.

results.result: Areal asymmetry is predominantly stable across the lifespan from age 4 to 89 years. Asymmetry was strongly established by age ~4, with largely parallel trajectories for both leftward and rightward asymmetries throughout life. There was little indication of relative hemispheric differences during cortical development (4-30 years) or aging (30-89 years), and areal asymmetry was significantly different from zero across the entire lifespan in all clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C36-C38 are supported by longitudinal lifespan trajectory analyses using GAMMs in the LCBC sample (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplements). The parallel trajectories and early establishment of asymmetry by age 4 are clearly demonstrated. The statistical analyses confirm asymmetry is significantly different from zero across the lifespan, supporting the interpretation of developmental stability.

results.result: Thickness asymmetry grows during childhood and peaks in early adulthood (median age ~24.3 years). Homotopic trajectories were non-parallel, characterized by developmental increase in thickness asymmetry from age 4-30 through unequal rates of continuous thinning between hemispheres. In 10/20 clusters, developmental increase corresponded to a significant relative hemispheric difference in the rate of developmental thinning, with the thicker hemisphere thinning comparatively slower. Despite this growth, 95% of clusters exhibited small but significant asymmetry already by age ~4.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C39-C43, C95 are supported by longitudinal trajectory analyses presented in Figures 3 and 4. The non-parallel trajectories, relative hemispheric differences in thinning rates, and age at peak asymmetry are quantitatively documented. The finding that asymmetry is already present at age 4 but continues to grow is well-supported by the GAMM analyses (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).

results.result: Most clusters did not exhibit relative hemispheric differences in rates of cortical thinning during aging (30-89 years), except in regions overlapping with previous reports (e.g., mPFC). This fits with previous work showing aging-related loss in thickness asymmetry is specific to heteromodal regions vulnerable in aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C104, C105 are supported by the relative aging trajectory analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5) and citations to prior work (Roe et al., 2021). The finding that most clusters do not show aging-related hemispheric differences is clearly documented, with exceptions noted in specific regions that overlap with previous analyses.

results.result: For areal asymmetry, a common covariance structure between asymmetries was detectable across datasets with correlation matrices correlating almost perfectly (r ≥ 0.97). The highest correlations reflected positive correlations between regions that are on average left-asymmetric and regions that are on average right-asymmetric. Opposite-direction areal asymmetries were more correlated if closer in cortex (geodesic distance), while same-direction asymmetries were not. These relationships could not be explained by brain size (ICV).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by Mantel tests and interregional correlation analyses presented in Figure 5A and 5C. The replication across three independent datasets (LCBC, UKB, HCP) with high correlation coefficients provides strong evidence. The geodesic distance analysis and ICV control analysis further support the specificity of these relationships.

results.result: For thickness asymmetry, a common covariance structure replicated across datasets (Mantel test r=0.46-0.62). Higher leftward asymmetry in left-asymmetric regions corresponded to more leftward asymmetry in right-asymmetric regions, and vice versa. PCA revealed PC1 explained 21.9% of variance in UKB, and there was a correlation of r=-0.61 between mean asymmetry across all leftward vs. rightward clusters. This indicates individuals may tend towards either leftward asymmetry, rightward asymmetry, or symmetry globally across the cortex, irrespective of the region-specific average direction of asymmetry.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54, C110 are supported by correlation analyses, Mantel tests, and PCA presented in Figure 5B, 5D, and supplementary figures. The pattern is most clear in UKB but replicates in LCBC and HCP. The interpretation of global directional tendencies is supported by the detailed inspection of correlations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and the PCA results.

results.result: Areal asymmetry is low-moderately heritable with maximum h2SNP approximately 19% in anterior insula. Global areal asymmetry heritability was substantially lower (h2SNP=7%, h2twin=16%) than hemispheric measures (h2SNP ~67%, h2twin ~92%). Four areal asymmetries showed significant twin-based heritability in HCP (19-27%), all of which were also significant in SNP-based analyses (8-19%). SNP-based analyses revealed 9/14 (64%) areal asymmetry clusters exhibited significant heritability.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C55-C59 are supported by heritability analyses using both SNP-based (UKB) and twin-based (HCP) methods. The convergence of results across methods and the specific identification of anterior insula as the most heritable region (h2SNP=18.6%) provide strong evidence. The contrast between high hemispheric heritability and low asymmetry heritability is well-documented.

results.result: Thickness asymmetry exhibits low or absent heritability. Only 3/20 (15%) thickness asymmetries exhibited significant SNP-based heritability (h2SNP=3-7%), and two robust asymmetries survived correction in twin-based analyses (rightward STS and lingual gyrus). Cluster-wise heritability estimates were significantly lower for thickness asymmetry than for area using a SNP-based approach (β=-1.1, p=0.0008) but not a twin-based approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C60-C62 are supported by heritability analyses presented in the manuscript and Supplementary file 1I. The low heritability of thickness asymmetry is consistently demonstrated across both SNP-based and twin-based methods, with statistical comparison confirming significantly lower heritability for thickness vs. area asymmetry in SNP-based analyses.

results.result: Cortex-wide heritability analysis revealed consistent patterns for areal asymmetry across SNP- and twin-based methods. In HCP, 69 parcels survived FDR-correction, 84% of which were also significant in SNP-based analysis. In UKB, 267 (53%) parcels exhibited significant SNP-based heritability. Higher heritability was observed in anterior insula, SMG, Sylvian fissure, STS, calcarine sulcus, cingulate, medial and orbitofrontal cortex, and fusiform, with spatial correlation r=0.46 between SNP- and twin-based maps. Maximum SNP-heritability was observed in anterior insula (16.4%).
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by cortex-wide heritability analyses presented in Figure 6A. The convergence of results across SNP- and twin-based methods, the high proportion of significant parcels, and the consistent spatial pattern provide strong evidence. The identification of anterior insula as the most heritable region is well-documented.

results.result: For thickness asymmetry, cortex-wide heritability was low and inconsistent between methods. Only 15 parcels survived FDR-correction in twin-based analysis, 7 of which were also significant in SNP-based analysis. Significant SNP-heritability was observed in only 11% (57) of parcels. There was little visual overlap in twin- and SNP-based heritability patterns (spatial correlation r=0.24). Cortex-wide heritability estimates were significantly lower for thickness asymmetry than for area using both SNP-based (β=-0.71, p<2.2e-16) and twin-based approaches (β=-0.33, p=1.08e-7).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by cortex-wide heritability analyses presented in Figure 6B. The low heritability, limited spatial extent of significant parcels, poor agreement between methods, and statistical comparison with areal asymmetry all provide converging evidence for low heritability of thickness asymmetry.

results.result: For areal asymmetry, large SNP-based genetic correlations explained several phenotypic correlations, including high correlations between leftward SMG/perisylvian and rightward lateral parietal cortex (rGSNP=0.83), leftward superior frontal cortex and rightward cingulate (rGSNP=0.82), and leftward anterior temporal/parahippocampal and rightward lateral parietal cortex (rGSNP=0.68). Two twin-based genetic correlations survived FDR-correction, including replication of the SMG/perisylvian - lateral parietal cortex correlation (rGtwin=1.0). For thickness asymmetry, only one post-corrected significant SNP-based genetic correlation was found (rGSNP=0.68).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 are supported by genetic correlation analyses presented in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The convergence of SNP-based and twin-based results for areal asymmetry, particularly the replication of the SMG/perisylvian - lateral parietal cortex correlation, provides strong evidence. The contrast with thickness asymmetry (only one significant correlation) is well-documented.

results.result: Higher areal asymmetry in the largest leftward cluster (SMG/perisylvian) was significantly associated with better general cognitive ability (β=0.03, p=7.4e-7) in UK Biobank. This association was far from the correction threshold and retained significance in the non-imputed subset.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C77 are supported by association analyses in UK Biobank data presented in Figure 7. The effect size is small but statistically robust, surviving Bonferroni correction and replication in the non-imputed subset. The authors appropriately note the small effect size and the association is with the most consistently lateralized region in humans (~94% of individuals show leftward asymmetry).

results.result: Reduced leftward areal asymmetry in anterior insula and thickness asymmetry along postcentral gyrus was evident in left-handers. Males typically exhibited slightly stronger areal asymmetry in large clusters (e.g., leftward SMG/perisylvian and temporal pole; rightward inferior parietal and superior frontal) but reduced asymmetry in mPFC. For thickness, males exhibited more rightward asymmetry in STS and posterior insula, more leftward asymmetry in superior frontal cortex, but reduced rightward asymmetry in entorhinal cortex and anterior insula.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 are supported by association analyses in UK Biobank data presented in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 1J-K. The handedness findings are consistent with prior work (Sha et al., 2021a). The sex effects are small but statistically significant and show region-specific patterns. All effects survived Bonferroni correction.

results.result: Areal asymmetry is developmentally stable and arises early in life through genetic but mainly subject-specific stochastic effects. Adult-like patterns of lateralization were strongly established before age ~4, indicating areal asymmetry traces back further and does not primarily emerge through later cortical expansion. This may align with evidence indicating areal asymmetry may be primarily determined in utero and fits with the principle that the primary microstructural basis of cortical area is determined in prenatal life. While heritability of either hemisphere was high, areal asymmetry heritability was only moderate at best, suggesting genetic but primarily subject-specific stochastic effects underlie its formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C87, C90-C93, C119, C121 represent an integrated interpretation of multiple findings: lifespan stability (C2, C36-C38), low-moderate heritability (C4, C55-C59), and early establishment by age 4. This interpretation is well-supported by the data and consistent with prior literature on prenatal brain development (Li et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2023; Rakic, 1995). The authors appropriately acknowledge that work linking prenatal and childhood trajectories is needed to affirm this interpretation (C87).

results.result: Childhood developmental growth shapes thickness asymmetry and may lead to directional variability of global thickness lateralization in the population. Developmental trajectories suggest differentiation of the cortex occurs with respect to thickness asymmetry in development, possibly suggesting it may be more amenable to experience-dependent change. Thickness asymmetry growth may suggest hemispheric differences in the developmental optimization of cortical networks at least partly shaped by childhood experience. This raises the possibility thickness asymmetry may be a marker of ontogenetic hemispheric specialization within neurocognitive networks. However, this is speculative, and intervention approaches are needed to experimentally test plasticity of thickness asymmetry in humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C88, C96-C99, C113, C114, C122 represent a speculative interpretation of the combined findings of developmental growth trajectories, low heritability, and global interrelations of thickness asymmetry. While the data support developmental growth and low heritability, the interpretation that this reflects experience-dependent plasticity is speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge this speculation (C99) and note that intervention approaches are needed to test this hypothesis. The interpretation is plausible but not directly demonstrated by the data.

results.result: For areal asymmetry, most asymmetries were either not or only weakly correlated, fitting with a multifaceted view and contrasting views emphasizing a single factor controlling cerebral lateralization. However, several regions wherein areal asymmetry reliably correlated within individuals were identified, showing the variance in cortical asymmetries is not always dissociable. Several of these were underpinned by high asymmetry-asymmetry SNP-based genetic correlations, illustrating some lateralizations in surface area exhibit coordinated genetic development.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by interregional correlation analyses (Figure 5A) and genetic correlation analyses (Figure 6C). The finding that most asymmetries are weakly correlated but some show strong correlations is well-documented. The genetic correlations provide mechanistic insight into the coordinated development of specific asymmetries.

results.result: The global interrelation of thickness asymmetry may be in broad agreement with the notion that some lateralized genetic-developmental programs may trigger lateralization in either direction or lose their directional bias through environmental interaction. As thickness asymmetry seems established at but minimal from birth, genetic effects may determine the average region-specific hemispheric bias in the population, but later developmental change may subsequently confer major increases upon its directional variance.
results.evaluation: Claims C111 and C112 are speculative interpretations of the thickness asymmetry findings. While the data support global interrelation, low heritability, and developmental growth, the specific interpretation regarding directional bias and environmental interaction is not directly tested. The interpretation is plausible and consistent with prior theories (Francks, 2015) but remains speculative.

results.result: Areal asymmetry in anterior insula is the most heritable asymmetry yet reported with genomic methods (h2SNP ~19%), notably higher than in a recent report (<5%). Highest SNP and twin-based heritability for areal asymmetry was found in regions constituting the earliest emerging cortical asymmetries in utero (anterior insula, STS, PT, medial occipital cortex, parahippocampal gyrus). The effects agree with and elaborate on two previous genetic explorations and reports of heritable areal asymmetry in handedness-associated clusters. Since asymmetry here emerges early in utero and is by far the most heritable, this ontogenetically foundational region of cortex may be fruitful for understanding genetic-developmental mechanisms influencing laterality.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118, C130 are supported by heritability analyses (Figure 6A) and citations to prior literature on prenatal brain development (Dubois et al., 2010; Habas et al., 2012; Kasprian et al., 2011; Hill et al., 2010). The identification of anterior insula as the most heritable region is well-documented, and the comparison to prior work (Sha et al., 2021a) demonstrates improvement in the approach. The interpretation regarding genetic-developmental mechanisms is reasonable given the convergence of heritability and prenatal development findings.

results.result: These results support a differentiation between early-life (i.e., before age ~4) and later developmental factors in shaping areal and thickness asymmetry, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 is a summary interpretation supported by the combined findings of lifespan stability and low-moderate heritability for areal asymmetry (C2, C4, C36-C38, C55-C59) versus developmental growth and low heritability for thickness asymmetry (C3, C6, C39-C43, C60-C62). This differentiation is a major conclusion of the study and is well-supported by the data.

results.result: The vertex-wise analysis of cortical asymmetries that reproduce across adult cohorts replicates and completes a recent low-resolution meta-analysis and can serve as a high-fidelity phenotype for future brain asymmetry studies. The marked consistency across samples suggests consensus may now be reached regarding cortical asymmetry phenotypes in humans. The high overlap in effects between seven datasets from four countries suggests these results likely apply universally. This evident consensus suggests genetic-developmental programs regulate mean brain lateralization with respect to both area and apparent thickness in humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are interpretations of the population-level asymmetry findings (C28-C35) in relation to prior literature. The high consistency across seven international datasets provides strong evidence for the universality of these asymmetry patterns. The interpretation that genetic-developmental programs regulate mean brain lateralization is supported by the consistency of patterns across samples, though the low heritability findings (C85) suggest these programs may have reached population fixation.

results.result: The genetic findings suggest cortical asymmetries may have reached population fixation, as heritability of even optimally delineated asymmetry measures was generally low. This indicates either subject-specific stochastic mechanisms in early neurodevelopment or later developmental influences primarily determine cortical asymmetry.
results.evaluation: Claims C85 and C86 are interpretations of the heritability findings (C4, C6, C55-C62). The low heritability despite consistent population-level patterns is well-documented. The interpretation that this indicates population fixation or subject-specific stochastic/developmental influences is reasonable, though the relative contributions of these factors remain to be determined.

results.result: The findings agree with work finding a similar left-right thickness asymmetry pattern shows rapid longitudinal increase in the first years of life, particularly in mPFC. As rapid asymmetry differentiation spanning childhood and adolescence was observed in most prefrontal regions and others, these findings extend earlier findings in neonates. Likely, longitudinal data and nonlinear modelling was critical to capture early developmental growth in thickness asymmetry within a lifespan perspective. As prefrontal thickness asymmetry seems particularly vulnerable in some neurodevelopmental disorders, aging, and Alzheimer's disease, these trajectories provide a useful normative reference regarding the timing of expected brain change in development.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are interpretations of the thickness asymmetry developmental findings (C3, C39-C43) in relation to prior literature (Li et al., 2015; Postema et al., 2019; Roe et al., 2021). The agreement with prior work and the extension to childhood and adolescence are well-supported. The interpretation regarding the importance of longitudinal data and nonlinear modelling is reasonable given the complexity of the trajectories. The clinical relevance is supported by citations to prior literature.

results.result: Since interhemispheric anatomy in the SMG/perisylvian region is likely related to brain torque, the association with cognitive ability may agree with work suggesting torque relates to cognitive outcomes. That ~94% of humans exhibit leftward asymmetry in this region suggests tightly regulated genetic-developmental programs control its lateralized direction in humans. This result may suggest disruptions in areal lateralization early in life are associated with cognitive deficits detectable in later life as small effects in big data. While speculative, this may also agree with evidence that differences in general cognitive ability that show high lifespan stability relate primarily to areal phenotypes formed early in life.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 are speculative interpretations of the cognitive association finding (C7, C77). While the association is statistically robust, the interpretation regarding brain torque, disruptions in early life, and cognitive deficits is speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge this speculation (C128) and cite relevant prior literature (Toga and Thompson, 2003; LeMay, 1976; Kong, 2019; Zhao et al., 2021; Deary et al., 2004; Walhovd et al., 2016; Rakic, 1995; Fjell et al., 2019). The interpretation is plausible but not directly demonstrated.

results.result: Anterior insula lies within a left-lateralized functional language network, and its structural asymmetry may relate to language lateralization in which left-handers show increased atypicality. Less leftward somatosensory thickness asymmetry in left-handers echoes a recent report and fits a scenario whereby thickness asymmetries may be partly shaped through use-dependent plasticity and detectable through group-level hemispheric specializations of function. Still, the small effects show cortical asymmetry cannot predict individual handedness. Associations with other factors typically assumed important were similarly small, and mostly compatible with prior reports. Possibly, differences in sample median age and potential sex-differences in brain decline may underlie some inconsistencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C129, C131-C134 are interpretations of the handedness and sex association findings (C78-C80) in relation to prior literature. The associations are statistically significant but small, as appropriately noted. The interpretation regarding language lateralization and use-dependent plasticity is supported by citations to prior literature (Labache et al., 2019; Chiarello et al., 2013; Biduła and Króliczak, 2015; Keller et al., 2011; Wiberg et al., 2019; Mazoyer et al., 2014; Westerhausen et al., 2006; Carey and Johnstone, 2014; Sha et al., 2021a). The acknowledgment that cortical asymmetry cannot predict individual handedness is appropriate given the small effect sizes.
